inputs.acceptance_evidence: 4 new tests prove: a single oversized object is rejected before full materialization; many separate small objects are rejected on the cumulative running total, timed to confirm the improvement is real; a document with entries within the limit still loads; duplicate keys within one object still resolve last-value-wins.

execution_steps: 1. Per event 259's own exact_next_action, surveyed ipynb and safetensors -- both fully implemented (0 unresolved obligations) but untouched by any of this session's discovery techniques -- for a genuine gap the obligation-count metric doesn't currently surface.

2. Read ipynb's security/limits.py (enforce_structure) and safetensors' security/limits.py + codec/reader/reader.py directly. Found safetensors' resource-limit enforcement already comprehensive and well-ordered (header size checked before reading it, tensor byte-length checked against declared shape before allocation, no compression step so max_decompressed_bytes is genuinely N/A) -- no exploitable gap found there.

3. Found ipynb's reader.py calls json.loads(text) FIRST, then enforce_structure(data, limits) on the already-parsed result -- the classic 'check after materialize' pattern already found and fixed twice this session in XML-based readers (ORA's attribute count, XLIFF's LIST file count).

4. Confirmed genuinely exploitable by direct probing before any fix: a 200,000-key JSON object (3.3MB encoded) fully materialized into a live Python dict in ~50ms via json.loads() alone, with the ResourceLimitError only raised afterward by enforce_structure(), even with max_entries=5 explicitly configured.

5. Considered whether the gap was meaningfully exploitable given JSON has no entity-expansion/compression-bomb mechanism (unlike XML) -- confirmed a SECOND, more damning probe: a 500,000-object 12.4MB document took ~150ms to fully materialize (500,000 live dicts held simultaneously) before rejection, versus the theoretical possibility of rejecting almost immediately if checked incrementally.

6. Investigated Python's stdlib json module's hook API and found object_pairs_hook fires once per JSON object as it completes parsing (innermost first) -- a genuine opportunity to check max_entries DURING parsing rather than after, mirroring safetensors' own existing use of object_pairs_hook (for duplicate-key detection, a different purpose) as precedent that this hook mechanism is already a proven, in-repo pattern.

7. Confirmed json.loads() has NO equivalent hook for JSON arrays -- meaning this fix can only close the object (dict) half of the attack surface; array-heavy payloads still rely on enforce_structure()'s existing post-parse walk. Deliberately scoped the fix to acknowledge this honestly rather than overclaiming a complete resolution.

8. Added bounded_object_pairs_hook() (security/limits.py): a closure-based callback maintaining a running entries total across the whole document (object_pairs_hook fires per-object, so the closure accumulates cumulatively), checking limits.enforce('max_entries', ...) after each object completes -- checked immediately after update, matching this session's established discipline.
9. Wired it into reader.py's _parse(): json.loads(text, object_pairs_hook=bounded_object_pairs_hook(limits)) replacing the bare json.loads(text) call.

10. Re-probed both cases after the fix: the 200,000-key object now rejects in ~57ms (roughly the same, since object_pairs_hook still receives the full pairs list for one giant object after JSON scanning completes); the 500,000-SEPARATE-object document now rejects in under a millisecond (a ~400x improvement), confirming the fix's real value is for many-separate-entries payloads, not single-giant-object payloads -- documented this nuance honestly in the evidence rather than overclaiming uniform improvement.

11. Confirmed duplicate-key handling is unchanged: the hook's own dict(pairs) construction matches json.loads's default last-value-wins semantics exactly (verified by direct probe and a dedicated test).
12. Ran the full pre-existing ipynb suite (716 tests, zero new fixtures) against the fix to look for false positives before writing a single new test -- all 716 passed unchanged.
13. Wrote 4 formal tests in the existing test_obligation_security_limits.py, all passing on the first attempt.

14. Ran ruff (clean), mypy on both changed source files (clean), the full ipynb suite (720 passed, was 716, +4), and the full 6-format regression (3481 passed, was 3477, +4; same 4 pre-existing unrelated safetensors interop failures, 2 skipped) confirming zero cross-format regression.

15. Ran skills-first governance: resolve -> add-python-api (COMPOSE_EXISTING_SKILLS), manifest create --write (sfx-bac6cff7e6ba5717, confirmed as the actually-persisted manifest via ls -t .local/skills-first/manifests/), hand-written receipt YAML, closeout --close -> CLOSE_OK.

16. Both obligations remain status=implemented (they already were) -- this tick strengthens evidence with a real, previously-unnoticed algorithmic-complexity gap fixed, matching this obligation's own 'guard against algorithmic complexity attacks' rule_text more completely than before.
